title: The TLS handshake
summary: How a browser gets an encrypted, authenticated channel before sending a single byte of HTTP.

steps.title: What TLS gives you
body: HTTPS is HTTP inside **TLS**. TLS gives three things:
- **Confidentiality**: nobody on the path can read the traffic.
- **Authentication**: you're really talking to `shop.example`, proven by its **certificate** chaining to a root you trust.
The certificate part is deep enough to have its own topic: see **Certificates & PKI** for chains, trust stores and what breaks them.

steps.prompt: An attacker on cafe Wi-Fi watches your HTTPS traffic to `shop.example`. What can they still learn?
options: The server's IP and (via SNI) the hostname, plus traffic sizes and timing
steps.explain: TLS hides everything inside the connection, but IPs, the SNI hostname (unless Encrypted Client Hello is used) and packet sizes stay visible.

steps.title: TLS 1.3 in one round trip
body: - Both sides combine **key shares** (ephemeral Diffie-Hellman) into the same secret without ever sending it: *forward secrecy*.
- **SNI** tells the server which site's certificate to present (many sites, one IP).

lines: ClientHello with SNI and key share
Client verifies the certificate chain and name
steps.explain: DNS, then TCP, then TLS, then HTTP. HTTP/3 merges the transport and TLS steps inside QUIC.

steps.prompt: Match each TLS term to its job.
pairs: Proves the server owns the name

steps.prompt: `curl https://10.0.0.5/` fails with *certificate subject name does not match*, but `curl https://shop.example/` (same IP) works. Why?
options: The certificate is for `shop.example`; connecting by IP checks the name `10.0.0.5`, and no SNI is sent
The server's TLS version is too old
steps.explain: Name checks compare the name you *asked for* with the certificate. Use the name (or `curl --resolve shop.example:443:10.0.0.5 https://shop.example/` to pin the IP).

steps.title: HSTS
body: Typing `shop.example` starts with plain `http://`. That first request can be intercepted and never redirected (SSL stripping).
**HSTS** closes the gap. Over HTTPS the server sends:
For `max-age` seconds the browser **rewrites every http:// URL for that host to https://** itself, before any packet leaves, and refuses to let users click through certificate errors.
`includeSubDomains` extends it to `*.shop.example`. `preload` asks to be built into browsers so even the very first visit is protected.
> **Tip:** start with a small max-age. If any subdomain can't do HTTPS, `includeSubDomains` breaks it for a year.

steps.prompt: Complete the header: enforce HTTPS for one year on this host and all subdomains.

steps.title: Parse HSTS
prompt: Write `(int MaxAge, bool IncludeSubDomains, bool Preload)` `ParseHsts(string header)`.
Directives are `;`-separated, case-insensitive, with optional spaces; `max-age` may be quoted (`max-age="600"`). A missing `max-age` throws `FormatException`.
starter: (int MaxAge, bool IncludeSubDomains, bool Preload) ParseHsts(string header)
solution: (int MaxAge, bool IncludeSubDomains, bool Preload) ParseHsts(string header)
foreach (var raw in header.Split(';', StringSplitOptions.RemoveEmptyEntries | StringSplitOptions.TrimEntries))
if (maxAge == null) throw new FormatException("max-age is required");
template: Dojo.Eq("full", (31536000, true, true), ParseHsts("max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains; preload"));
Dojo.Eq("quoted, odd case", (300, true, false), ParseHsts("MAX-AGE=\"300\" ;includesubdomains"));
